newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - W.Europe Jan car sales down, slow growth seen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - W.Europe Jan car sales down, slow growth seen.

text.p: New car sales in western Europe fell by 2.9 percent in January year-on-year, dragged down by plunging French registrations after the end last year of a state incentive scheme, the European Automobile Manufacturers Association (ACEA) said on Thursday.
New passenger car registrations declined to 1,130,000 in January from 1,164,000 the same month in 1996.
ACEA still sees growth for the whole of 1997 but much lower than the rise of 6.6 percent last year in the 15-member European Union, Norway, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
Spokesman James Rosenstein said car registrations were forecast to rise by a modest 1.8 percent in 1997.
However, this was a "guarded estimate of probable growth" and the figure could turn out to be lower.
"Nobody expects strong growth," Rosenstein told Reuters, stressing that this was the year that EU countries were scrambling to meet tough economic criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU).
"Growth last year was slightly higher than we expected and that growth was driven by what we think is largely temporary factors in a number of countries," he said.
In a somewhat more optimistic forecast this week, investment bank Salomon Brothers said the European car market should grow by three percent this year and in 1998.
"We remain confident that volumes will move ahead this year with strong Italian sales and in the grip of incentives and weak French sales in their aftermath," it said in a report.
But, it warned, "market growth is unlikely to lift Europe out of the price competition which has intensified over the year end."
The ACEA figures for last month showed wide variations among the 18 countries included in the survey.
Car registrations plunged 33.7 percent in France and by 26.3 percent in Switzerland, but they soared by 28.4 percent in Sweden, 22.1 percent in Spain and 20.7 percent in Ireland.
Rosenstein said the European car market was fragmented and volatile. "There are different factors affecting different national markets."
Sales in France fell by 62,200 cars to 122,300.

"At the end of the year in France sales started to slide because the incentive was phased out but still for the year growth was strong. If you look at this year the incentive is gone in France so you have a very strong drop," he said.

The Volkswagen group -- including Audi, Seat and Skoda -- strengthened its position as Europe's leading car maker, increasing its market share to 17.2 percent from 16.8 percent in January last year, even though its total sales declined marginally by 0.1 percent to 194,800.

Italy's Fiat group, including Lancia and Alfa Romeo, saw its car registrations fall by 3.1 percent to 146,500 but held on to its market share of 13 percent, making it the second biggest car group on the west European market.
It was just ahead of U.S. car giants GM and Ford, which had 12.6 and 11.8 percent of the market respectively.
France's PSA, which includes Peugeot and Citroen, had 12.3 percent lower sales and its market share fell to 10.7 percent from 11.8 percent.
Japanese car makers, however, increased their share to 10.7 from 10.1 percent.
